newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Crippled Mir has good news after spate of trouble.
newsitem.headline: Crippled Mir has good news after spate of trouble.

text.p: The Russian-U.S. crew aboard the crippled Mir station had some good news on Sunday after the worst trouble in its 11-year history.

A mission control expert told Reuters the latest navigation problem of the station has been fixed and gyrodines -- the devices that keep its solar panels lined up to the Sun to gain maximum power -- were now working.
"Yesterday evening all 12 gyrodines have been put into motion and they now work in a stable manner," the expert, who declined to be named, said by telephone.
The specialist did not say how the devices had been repaired and who -- mission control by remote commands or the three-men Russian-U.S. crew carried out the repair works.

Deputy mission chief Sergei Krikalyov said on Thursday there had been an unexplained malfunction in all of the station's gyrodines. The result was that the cosmonauts had to fire their rocket engines to keep Mir lined up to the Sun and prevent a further loss of electric power.
The station lost up to half its power on June 25 after a collision with an unmanned cargo craft punctured the Spektr scientific module and cut off supplies from some panels.
It was the worst accident since Mir was first blasted into its orbit around the Earth more than 11 years ago.

A cargo craft is on the way to Mir with relief supplies and is expected to dock with the ageing station on Monday. The expert said the cosmonauts were resting on Sunday to accumulate energy for the docking.
Commander Vasily Tsibliyev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin of Russia and British-born U.S. astronaut Michael Foale were all feeling fine, he said.

The expert also said the Progress cargo craft, launched on Saturday from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan which Russia leases, has coped with a problem it had encountered when it took off -- a panel of a solar battery did not unfold properly.
"It unfolded fully today and the ship is getting 100 percent energy," he said. "All systems of the Progress work normally."

The supplies aboard the unmanned Progress M-35 include oxygen, food and water as well as repair tools. Experts say the overall lack of power on Mir will make the docking operation for Progress problematic.

The fixing of the gyrodines followed the latest bout of trouble which happened on Tuesday but was disclosed only on Saturday when Russian and NASA officials confirmed that there had been a mystery leak from the holed Spektr module.

A Russian specialist said: "Five days ago, in one of our communications with the crew, we were told they had seen flakes and bubbles from an unknown source leaking from the Spektr module." He added it was not fuel.
The leak had been into space rather than inside, and there had been no repeat since that single incident.

It highlighted the dangers facing the crew during a sortie to Spektr on July 17 or 18 when Tsibliev and Lazutkin plan to enter the crippled module in their space suits to reconnect electrical cables and restore some power lost after the crash.
Michael Foale is to sit out the repair inside the station's emergency escape ship.

"We are very concerned about what was in that module, what might have ruptured, and what the impact might be on the suited crew members," veteran astronaut Frank Culbertson, who runs NASA's missions to Mir, told a news conference.

There are concerns the cosmonauts could get toxic materials on their spacesuits during the repair. NASA and Russian space officials were trying to determine what dangerous materials might be present inside Spektr, Culbertson said.

The white flakes seen escaping from Mir on Tuesday may have been caused by something bursting inside the module and leaking through the station's ruptured hull or could have come from a damaged radiator on the exterior of the module, he said.
